findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and why it matters, in plain words. This part works well.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The second section is a visible failure. The lede promises a commit traced to "the models, the cost and the verdict", and the only place that would show this shows an error, so a newcomer sees no proof of Athena's main selling point.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: At doodla.github.io/athena a newcomer expects Athena's home page, but almost all of the page describes a different tool, firstmate. The lede explains why (the study is a demonstration), but the reader has to work out that firstmate's states, transitions and 45 claims are an example and not something they need to learn.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and lede "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project..."

findings.text: A heading called "Start here" on Athena's site starts with firstmate, not Athena. A newcomer could read it as a guide to getting started with Athena.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work..."

findings.text: The next step is easy to find from the top, and it is concrete: prerequisites, a clone command, an install command and a first request to try. A newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and Next steps: "git clone https://github.com/doodla/athena.git", "./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page does not say whether Athena needs a paid model account or API key, or which operating systems it supports. A newcomer could install it and only then find out they cannot run it.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm (to install Claude Code)"

findings.text: This link is for the site owner, yet it appears in the newcomer's first screen with no explanation of who "you" is. It is a distraction for a first-time reader.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The traceability is real and you can check it: every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to file lines at a pinned commit. This backs up the claim in the lede, but the citation markers on nearly every line make the page dense for a casual reader.
findings.source: Each statement ends in claim ids such as "[c1] [c11] [c21] [c22]"; Claims and sources links to lines like "AGENTS.md:206-206"
